Chapter 30

Rate limits and pagination

A token bucket with no timers, and cursors that do not silently drop rows when the tape moves.

By the end of this chapter

Protect the venue from one client, and page through a moving list correctly.

The simpler thing, and its hole

The obvious limiter is a counter per minute: allow sixty, reset on the minute. Three lines, and you can drive a lorry through it.

A client sends sixty requests at 11:00:59 and sixty more at 11:01:00. Two counters, both within limit, one hundred and twenty requests in one second. The venue sees exactly the burst the limit existed to prevent, and the "requests per minute" graph says everything is fine.

The token bucket

A bucket holds tokens. Each request costs one. Tokens refill at a steady rate, and the bucket has a ceiling. That gives you two knobs that mean genuinely different things:

  • Refill rate — the sustained throughput you are willing to serve.
  • Capacity — how much burst you tolerate from a client that has been quiet.

Why burst tolerance is not generosity

A market maker who sits still for a minute and then cancels forty orders because the market moved is doing something entirely reasonable, and a flat counter punishes them for it. The capacity knob lets you say "sustained twenty a second, but I will forgive a hundred at once from somebody who has been idle" — which is a sentence about how markets actually behave.

No timers

The bucket does not refill on a schedule. It works out how much time has passed since it was last touched and adds that much, at the moment somebody asks.

Ten thousand idle keys cost ten thousand small objects and zero scheduled work. With a timer per key they would cost ten thousand wakeups a second to do nothing at all.

now is a parameter. The tests drive time by passing numbers rather than by sleeping — a rate-limit suite built on setTimeout is slow, flaky on a loaded CI box, and cannot check the interesting cases at all.

Authenticate first, then limit

The bucket is keyed on the credential, which means it can only be keyed on something we have already verified. Limit first and unauthenticated traffic all shares one bucket — one broken client then locks every other client out, which is a denial of service the limiter itself provides.

The cost of that ordering is that a flood of *invalid* credentials is not limited here. That belongs at the edge, in front of the app, where it can be dropped without a database round trip. Saying so is better than pretending one limiter solves both problems.

This limiter is in-memory and therefore per-process. Two web servers behind a load balancer give a client two buckets. That is a deliberate limit, not an oversight — a shared limiter needs Redis or similar in the request path — but you must know it is true before you rely on the number.

Cursors, not offsets

LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100 is correct only if the list does not change between requests. The trade tape changes several times a second.

Twenty new trades arrive while a client is on page two, everything shifts down twenty rows, and page three re-serves twenty rows the client already has — or, going the other way, skips twenty it will never see. A reconciliation built on that is quietly wrong, and nothing errors.

A cursor encodes where you actually were: the sequence number and id of the last row you saw. The next page is "everything after that", which is stable no matter what arrives in between.

Refuse a bad cursor loudly

The tempting behaviour is to treat an unparseable cursor as "start from the beginning". It never errors, so it looks robust. What it actually does is put a client that corrupted its cursor into an infinite loop, re-reading page one forever and reporting no problem. Silently doing something reasonable is the most expensive kind of forgiveness.

Filter in SQL, not in JavaScript

Note also what this endpoint does not return: the counterparty. In a centrally cleared market the counterparty is the clearing house, and telling Northgate they just bought from Lowfield hands them information they would pay for and are not entitled to.

  • You can explain what refill rate and capacity each control

  • You can explain why offset pagination is wrong on a moving list, and why a bad cursor errors
